areas.summary: By late 2026, recording which code an agent wrote has split into three layers. First, plain-text markers in commits: Co-Authored-By, Assisted-by or Generated-by trailers, bot authors, and session-log URL trailers. Second, line-level recorders such as Git AI (its founders were hired by OpenAI) and the Agent Trace RFC from Cursor, Cognition and others, which store data in git notes or sidecar files. Third, cryptographic layers: signed bot commits, gitsign/Sigstore with workload identity, and SLSA/in-toto attestations. Signed attestations are mostly vendor guidance and young projects, not established practice. The main negative result came from the Linux kernel. Only about 10% of 18,533 commits carried the Assisted-by tag, so the kernel dropped it in October 2026; human Signed-off-by stays, and disclosure moved to the cover letter. Census studies agree: trailer and bot signals capture a fraction of agent activity, and detectors without those signals reach only 0.33 precision. Package hallucination has been measured repeatedly. 2026 frontier models hallucinate 3.6-6% of package mentions, and 53 names shared across vendors could still be registered. The consensus defense is an install-time dependency firewall (Socket sfw, Aikido Safe Chain, GitHub package firewall), not better models. Legal status is mostly settled at the edges and open in the middle. Purely AI output is not copyrightable in the US (Thaler; Copyright Office Part 2), and the Ninth Circuit rejected DMCA 1202 output claims in Doe v. GitHub. Contract claims and the input-side DMCA theory remain open, open-source projects are split from bans (QEMU, Gentoo, NetBSD) to disclosure-only policies, and vendor IP indemnities usually lapse once you edit or combine the output.

approaches.name: Commit-message trailers and bot authorship
approaches.description: Free-text markers in git history: Co-Authored-By, Assisted-by or Generated-by trailers, agent bot accounts as author with the human as co-author, and URL trailers pointing to session logs. Cheap and searchable, but they prove nothing cryptographically, users can strip them, and compliance is low.
candidates: Linux kernel AI Coding Assistants policy and Assisted-by removal
Claude Code attribution setting and co-author controversy
GitHub Copilot cloud agent signed commits + Agent-Logs-Url trailer

approaches.name: Line-level session recorders (agent hooks + git notes / sidecar)
approaches.description: Agent hooks checkpoint each edit as AI or human. At commit time an authorship log is attached as a git note or a JSONL sidecar, and it is rewritten across rebase, squash and cherry-pick. This gives line-level AI blame. It cannot cover code written before installation, or edits made outside the hooks.
candidates: agentdiff / Agent Blame / Semantica (via repowise survey)

approaches.name: Cryptographic agent identity and commit signing
approaches.description: Bind the commit to an identity the agent cannot forge: platform-signed bot commits, gitsign keyless signing with an OIDC or SPIFFE workload identity, and the Rekor transparency log. A signature proves which key or workflow made the commit, not which model wrote the diff.
candidates: GitHub Copilot cloud agent signed commits + Agent-Logs-Url trailer

approaches.name: SLSA / in-toto / AIBOM attestation of agent runs
approaches.description: Describe the agent run as a build: model, prompt digest, skills, base commit and approver as resolvedDependencies or externalParameters, signed by a runner the agent cannot reach. Optionally add an AI-BOM in CycloneDX or SPDX 3. This is mostly guidance and early implementations, and no standard buildType exists for agent runs.
candidates: Safeguard: provenance and AIBOM for agent-made code
Factory: build provenance for coding agent artifacts

approaches.name: Inference and detection from history
approaches.description: Estimate agent authorship after the fact from bot accounts, trailers, config files and behavioral fingerprints. Useful for research and audits of existing repos. Precision drops sharply once self-disclosed markers are removed.
candidates: Detecting AI Coding Agents in Open Source: census of 180M repos
Agent or Human? signature-free commit detection

approaches.name: Install-time dependency firewall against slopsquatting
approaches.description: A proxy or wrapper around npm, pip, uv or cargo that checks every package, including transitive ones, against a malware feed and a minimum-age cooldown before download. It is applied to agents via a PATH wrapper, a PreToolUse hook, or the platform default. It does not depend on the model getting names right.
candidates: boda.sh supply-chain security in coding agents

approaches.name: Measuring package hallucination and inference-time mitigation
approaches.description: Benchmarks of how often models invent package names, how persistent and shared across models those names are, and which decoding, RAG or self-refine defenses reduce the rate.
candidates: The Range Shrinks, the Threat Remains (2026 frontier replication)
Evaluating Inference-Time Defenses against Package Hallucination (ASE 2026)
Setup Complete, Now You Are Compromised

approaches.name: License contamination detection (memorization + snippet scanning)
approaches.description: Measure how often models reproduce licensed code verbatim, and catch it in CI with snippet-matching scanners or vendor public-code filters.
candidates: GitHub Copilot public-code matching in agent session logs

approaches.name: Project contribution policies (DCO-centric)
approaches.description: Open-source projects decide whether AI output can satisfy the DCO or CLA. Positions range from a ban (QEMU, Gentoo, NetBSD), to accepting it with human Signed-off-by plus disclosure (kernel, Fedora, ASF, OpenInfra), to strict disclosure with public denouncement of offenders (Ghostty).
candidates: Linux kernel AI Coding Assistants policy and Assisted-by removal

approaches.name: Legal status and contractual risk transfer
approaches.description: Copyrightability (human-authorship requirement in the US; UK proposal to drop s9(3)), infringement and DMCA claims over regurgitated code, and vendor IP indemnities with carve-outs for modified or combined output.
candidates: US Copyright Office Part 2 + Thaler v. Perlmutter
Vendor IP indemnity comparison (Microsoft CCC, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google)
UK Report on Copyright and AI (March 2026)

candidates.name: Agent Trace spec
candidates.claim: Vendor-neutral RFC v0.1.0 for line-level attribution of AI code. A JSON trace record maps file ranges to a conversation URL, a contributor type (human, ai, mixed, unknown) and a model_id. It supports git, jj and hg and optional content hashes, and leaves storage open. It is backed by Cursor, Cognition, Cloudflare, Vercel, Jules, Amp, OpenCode and git-ai, and has a TypeScript reference implementation writing .agent-trace/traces.jsonl.
candidates.limits: Explicit non-goals: legal ownership and training-data provenance. There is no standard reader or blame tooling yet. Line numbers are only valid at the recorded revision. Attribution is self-reported by agent hooks, so there is no tamper evidence. Thoughtworks rates it 'Assess'.
candidates.why: The one cross-vendor format: if a solo dev's harness emits it, attribution survives a switch between Claude Code, Codex and Cursor. Cheap to emit from a hook.

candidates.name: Git AI (git-ai-project)
candidates.claim: Apache-2.0 git extension. Agent hooks call 'git ai checkpoint'. On commit it writes line-level authorship to refs/notes/ai and rewrites notes after rebase, squash, cherry-pick, stash and reset. It provides AI blame and per-commit stats, works with about 12 local agents plus background agents, and claims about 2.6k GitHub stars. Its founders were hired by OpenAI's Codex team.
candidates.limits: Its own docs list gaps: git mv and copy-paste can lose attribution, and formatters and undo may flip lines to human. It relies on explicit agent hooks, so edits outside hooks are missed. The OpenAI hiring raises a vendor-neutrality question.
candidates.why: The most mature open-source recorder. Git notes keep history clean, which suits many parallel agents in worktrees across personal and employer repos.

candidates.name: Git AI joins OpenAI
candidates.claim: Git AI's founders join OpenAI Codex to measure Codex ROI. The open-source project is stated to continue.
candidates.limits: Only seen in a search snippet. Long-term neutrality and maintenance are unknown.
candidates.why: A major recorder now sits inside one agent vendor. Watch whether it stays cross-agent.

candidates.name: Linux kernel AI Coding Assistants policy and Assisted-by removal
candidates.claim: The kernel required 'Assisted-by: AGENT:MODEL' from 7.0, simplified it to 'Assisted-by: LLM' in 7.3, then removed it after the 2026 Maintainers Summit. Only about 10% of 18,533 non-merge commits in 7.3 through rc7 carried the tag, while LLM use was far wider. The rule 'AI agents MUST NOT add Signed-off-by' stays, and generated-content.rst still asks for disclosure in the cover letter.
candidates.limits: The 10% figure comes from the removal commit message, and nobody measured the true rate of AI use. Consensus was not unanimous (Pinchart objected). The kernel uses email patch flow, unlike PR-based projects.
candidates.why: The strongest real-world evidence that voluntary per-commit disclosure tags do not work at scale. It argues for tooling-emitted attribution instead.

candidates.name: Kernel Guidelines for Tool-Generated Content
candidates.claim: Asks submitters to disclose tools, their inputs (prompts or a prompt summary), the parts affected and how the change was tested whenever a meaningful amount of content was not written by someone in the Signed-off-by chain. Maintainers may reject submissions or give them extra scrutiny.
candidates.limits: Not enforced, and left to maintainers' discretion.
candidates.why: A ready template for what an agent's PR description should disclose.

candidates.name: Claude Code attribution setting and co-author controversy
candidates.claim: Claude Code appends 'Co-Authored-By: <model> <noreply@anthropic.com>' and a PR byline by default, and sessionUrl adds a claude.ai link. Opt-out is through the attribution.commit, pr and sessionUrl settings. Linked issues report trailers overriding CLAUDE.md, a third-party GitHub account matching an old claude-code@anthropic.com email (#58479), and an argument that a co-author trailer contradicts Copyright Office guidance (#66602).
candidates.limits: These are user complaints. The behavior changes across versions, with three separate keys and a deprecated includeCoAuthoredBy.
candidates.why: Directly affects a solo dev's commits. Defaults leak branding and session URLs into employer repos unless configured per repo.

candidates.name: Reporails: repos split on Co-Authored-By
candidates.claim: Among the 10,000 most-starred repos, about 465 have instruction-file rules against AI co-author trailers and about 330 ask for one (often Assisted-by). 64 disable attribution in committed Claude Code settings. Cursor's 'Made with Cursor' trailer cannot be removed by rules.
candidates.limits: Counts come from regex matches before hand-checking. The method is lightly described.
candidates.why: Shows there is no norm. Each repo needs an explicit policy in AGENTS.md or settings.

candidates.name: GitHub Copilot cloud agent signed commits + Agent-Logs-Url trailer
candidates.claim: Copilot cloud agent commits are authored by Copilot, with the human who assigned the task as co-author. Commits are platform-signed and show as Verified, and each carries an Agent-Logs-Url trailer linking to the session logs. Public-code matches are shown in the logs.
candidates.limits: Works only inside GitHub's hosted agent. Session logs live in GitHub, not in git. Public-code matching can still emit matching code even when the setting is Block.
candidates.why: A reference design (bot author + human co-author + signature + log link) worth copying in a self-hosted harness.

candidates.name: Detecting AI Coding Agents in Open Source: census of 180M repos
candidates.claim: Multi-method detection over World of Code (config files, commit messages, author identity, bot signatures). Bot-account lookup finds only 3.3% of 850,157 Claude Code commits, a 30x recall gap. Agents produce over 320k commits per month. PR-based and commit-based censuses capture nearly disjoint populations: Codex leads in PRs, Claude Code in commits.
candidates.limits: The union is a lower bound with unknown absolute recall. Only 4.8% of labeled Type B true positives were trailer-only commits.
candidates.why: Quantifies how unreliable any single attribution signal is.

candidates.name: Agent or Human? signature-free commit detection
candidates.claim: On 7.8M commits from 1,226 repos with signatures masked, detectors reach ROC AUC up to 0.859, but precision is at most 0.332 at the real agent share of 5.9%. The signal comes mostly from message verbosity and change size. It transfers poorly to held-out Claude Code (TF-IDF AUC 0.524).
candidates.limits: Labels come from signatures, which are themselves a lower bound.
candidates.why: A negative result: post-hoc detection cannot replace recorded attribution.

candidates.name: AgenTag
candidates.claim: Open-world attribution of agent PRs from behavioral fingerprints on AIDev (33,580 agent PRs). With markers stripped, Claude Code F1 is only 0.446, versus 0.717 with trailers. Codex and Copilot are identified with F1 above 0.97.
candidates.limits: Closed dataset of five agents, with an imbalanced class distribution.
candidates.why: Research-grade, not an operational tool.

candidates.name: Spracklen et al. USENIX Security 2025
candidates.claim: 16 models and 576k samples in Python and JavaScript. Hallucinated packages average 5.2% for commercial models and 21.7% for open-source ones, with 205,474 unique fake names. 43% of hallucinations repeat on all 10 reruns.
candidates.limits: 2024-era models. Later work shows standard-library modules inflate the rates.
candidates.why: The baseline that defined slopsquatting.

candidates.name: The Range Shrinks, the Threat Remains (2026 frontier replication)
candidates.claim: Replicates Spracklen on five 2026 models (Claude Sonnet 4.6, Haiku 4.5, GPT-5.4-mini, Gemini 2.5 Pro, DeepSeek V3.2) over 199,840 generations. Hallucination rate is 3.6-5.0% of mentions after live-registry revalidation, and the open-weight gap has disappeared. 104 names are hallucinated by all five models. About 1% of hallucinated names were registered within six months, and at least one was registered with malware.
candidates.limits: Independent preprint, not peer reviewed. GPT-5.4-mini refused 32% of prompts.
candidates.why: A current-model number: a solo dev's agents will still invent about 1 in 20 package names.

candidates.name: Socket: 53 slopsquatting targets across frontier LLMs
candidates.claim: Socket and PyPI Security reviewed the 127 cross-model names. 6 npm entries were false positives (Ember imports), PyPI blocklists covered 68, and 53 names were still registrable as of April 2026.
candidates.limits: Vendor blog with a commercial interest. Reports targets, not attacks.
candidates.why: Shows that registry-side protections (PyPI prohibited names) already absorb much of the risk.

candidates.name: Evaluating Inference-Time Defenses against Package Hallucination (ASE 2026)
candidates.claim: Prior methods inflated Python hallucination rates by up to 9.4 percentage points by counting stdlib modules. RAG reduces the rate in 18 of 32 model-language configurations. Adversarial prompts seeded with fake names raise the rate by up to 45 points, and Ruby reaches 80.9-95.2%.
candidates.limits: Eight models, mostly open-weight. Decoding defenses are not applicable to closed APIs.
candidates.why: Shows prompt-injected fake dependency names are the real threat for agents reading READMEs.

candidates.name: Setup Complete, Now You Are Compromised
candidates.claim: Microsoft researchers tested 12 scenarios in 5 attack classes, delivered through README, requirements and Makefile edits, across production agent harnesses. The same model catches an attack in one harness and installs it in another. Separator-confusion names (azurecore) slip through, and registry redirection is missed almost everywhere, including npm and Cargo.
candidates.limits: Small scenario set. Harness versions change fast.
candidates.why: Directly models a solo dev cloning repos and letting agents run setup. It argues for a harness-level gate rather than trusting the model.

candidates.name: Lasso huggingface-cli experiment
candidates.claim: About 48k how-to questions across 4 models and 5 languages, with hallucinations in 22-64% of answers. An empty PyPI package registered under the hallucinated name huggingface-cli got over 30k authentic downloads in 3 months, and an Alibaba repo README told users to install it.
candidates.limits: Download counts are hard to de-noise. 2023-24 models.
candidates.why: The canonical real-world demonstration that hallucinated names do get installed.

candidates.name: CSA research note on slopsquatting
candidates.claim: Collects confirmed cases, such as the malicious 'unused-imports' npm package (hallucinated for eslint-plugin-unused-imports) at about 233 weekly downloads in February 2026. Recommends lockfile pinning and a ban on agents installing without an allowlist or review.
candidates.limits: Secondary synthesis that leans on vendor reports.
candidates.why: A list of real incidents for threat modeling.

candidates.name: Socket Firewall (sfw)
candidates.claim: Free CLI with no API key. An ephemeral HTTP proxy wraps npm, yarn, pnpm, pip, uv and cargo and blocks known-malicious packages, including transitive ones, before download. Used in Replit's default Package Firewall.
candidates.limits: Blocks only known or flagged malware. The free tier only warns on AI-detected malware. A fresh slopsquat registered minutes ago may pass.
candidates.why: Easy to enforce for every agent through a PATH wrapper or a PreToolUse hook on a VPS and a Mac.

candidates.name: Aikido Safe Chain
candidates.claim: Free open-source local proxy for 16 package managers (npm, pnpm, bun, pip, uv, poetry and others). It checks against the AGPL Aikido Intel feed and enforces a minimum package age by hiding versions that are too new.
candidates.limits: Depends on feed latency (Aikido claims about 6 minutes on average). MCP servers and IDE extensions bypass it.
candidates.why: The minimum-age cooldown directly defeats freshly registered slopsquats, and it is open source.

candidates.name: GitHub package firewall (public preview)
candidates.claim: Install-time policy gate between agents or CI and upstream registries, with configurable cooldown, Advisory Database malware checks and attestation-downgrade checks. Explicitly motivated by agents installing without a human in the loop.
candidates.limits: GitHub Enterprise Cloud only, in preview.
candidates.why: Signals that cooldown plus attestation checks are becoming platform defaults.

candidates.name: boda.sh supply-chain security in coding agents
candidates.claim: Recipe for forcing sfw on agents in three ways: a PATH wrapper, a SKILL or AGENTS.md instruction, or a Claude Code PreToolUse hook that rewrites install commands.
candidates.limits: No measurement of bypass rates. Prompt-based enforcement is weak.
candidates.why: A copy-pasteable harness pattern for exactly this setup.

candidates.name: Safeguard: provenance and AIBOM for agent-made code
candidates.claim: A clear table of what each mark proves: a trailer proves nothing, a signed commit proves the key not the model, and only a runner-signed in-toto/SLSA attestation the agent cannot reach can bind inputs, model and approver. Proposes a custom buildType that maps task, skills and model into SLSA fields, and the SPDX 3.0.1 delegatedTo and invokedBy relations.
candidates.limits: Guidance only, with no shipped tool. Warns against claiming SLSA levels.
candidates.why: The best conceptual map of the trust gap between labels and attestations.

candidates.name: Factory: build provenance for coding agent artifacts
candidates.claim: Never accept binaries built in the agent session. CI rebuilds from the approved commit and emits a SLSA attestation, signing stays outside the agent prompt, and missing provenance is rejected.
candidates.limits: Short vendor guidance with no data.
candidates.why: A simple rule that applies to agent-driven deploys.

candidates.name: hummbl agent-provenance
candidates.claim: Python tool with zero dependencies. Adds Agent-Identity, Agent-Model, Attestation-Digest and Attestation-Signature trailers and exports an in-toto v1 statement with a SLSA predicate claiming Build L3.
candidates.limits: A single commit and no adoption. The L3 claim is doubtful because the agent signs its own provenance.
candidates.why: An example of the pattern, but immature and making overstated claims.

candidates.name: OpenFab (TODO Group)
candidates.claim: Apache-2.0 experiment: request, spec with checkable acceptance criteria, code, checks, then a signed AI-BOM (in-toto, SLSA, Sigstore, DIDs) with N-of-M human approval recorded as evidence. Presented to the TODO Group OSPO working group.
candidates.limits: Experimental, with no adoption data. The AI-BOM scope is described as an open question.
candidates.why: The most complete end-to-end design of agent output attestation, including human approval.

candidates.name: gitsign / Sigstore keyless signing
candidates.claim: Signs commits with short-lived Fulcio certificates bound to an OIDC identity and logs them in Rekor. Token providers include github-actions, spiffe, buildkite-agent and filesystem, so a non-human agent workflow can sign as itself.
candidates.limits: GitHub shows these signatures as Unverified. Verification happens out of band, and the commit becomes dependent on network access.
candidates.why: The practical way to give each agent runner its own verifiable signing identity without long-lived keys.

candidates.name: nucleus SPIFFE agent identity design
candidates.claim: Design note: the agent's SPIFFE SVID is exchanged for a short-lived repo-scoped GitHub App token, and commits are signed with gitsign, where the Fulcio SAN is the agent's SPIFFE ID. Candidly lists costs: no Verified badge, a self-hosted Fulcio is required, and JWT-SVID emission is missing.
candidates.limits: A design document, not shipped.
candidates.why: Rare honest accounting of what per-agent cryptographic identity costs.

candidates.name: Red Hat Rossoctl agent provenance
candidates.claim: Two-layer trust for agent cards: Sigstore signing in CI with SLSA provenance at build time, plus SPIFFE/SPIRE at runtime, verified in a Kubernetes operator.
candidates.limits: About agent artifacts (agent cards), not code the agents wrote.
candidates.why: Kubernetes-scale. Adjacent to identity of the agents themselves.

candidates.name: QEMU code provenance policy
candidates.claim: QEMU declines any contribution believed to include AI-generated content, on DCO grounds: clauses (b) and (c) cannot be certified for LLM output. A November 2026 relax-patch proposing four tiers (small fixes, pre-arranged large contributions) is contested on qemu-devel.
candidates.limits: Trust-based enforcement. The policy is in flux.
candidates.why: The clearest statement of the DCO argument against AI code.

candidates.name: Gentoo/NetBSD bans
candidates.claim: NetBSD presumes LLM code is 'tainted' and requires written core approval. Gentoo's council banned NLP-AI content on 2024-04-14 for copyright, quality and ethics reasons.
candidates.limits: Not enforced by detection.
candidates.why: Context for the policy spectrum, with little operational impact on a solo dev.

candidates.name: ASF Generative Tooling Guidance
candidates.claim: AI code is allowed if the tool's terms of use are compatible with the OSD, and either the output is uncopyrightable, it contains no third-party material, or any such material is used under a compatible license. Recommends a 'Generated-by:' token for a future machine-readable Tooling-Provenance file. Notes that ICLA s7 is impractical because sources are unknowable.
candidates.limits: Admits reasonable certainty is often unachievable because scanners only match known open-source code.
candidates.why: A usable checklist for when agent-written code goes into licensed projects.

candidates.name: OpenInfra AI policy
candidates.claim: Five pillars: AI welcome, humans accountable via DCO, material AI use disclosed in machine-readable labels (Assisted-By preferred over Generated-By), output understandable by humans, same quality bar. Purely autonomous submissions without an accountable human are not acceptable.
candidates.limits: Labels are voluntary.
candidates.why: Explicitly addresses autonomous agent submissions.

candidates.name: Fedora AI-Assisted Contributions Policy
candidates.claim: Disclosure via an Assisted-by trailer is mandatory when a significant part is taken from a tool unchanged. AI cannot be the final arbiter in reviews.
candidates.limits: Voluntary disclosure, likely to show the same low compliance as the kernel.
candidates.why: Part of the converging Assisted-by convention.

candidates.name: Ghostty AI_POLICY
candidates.claim: All AI use must be disclosed with the tool and its extent. Contributors who submit low-quality AI work ('slop') go on a public denouncement list. Maintainers are exempt.
candidates.limits: Social enforcement, which raises fairness concerns.
candidates.why: An example of a punitive norm.

candidates.name: melissawm open-source-ai-contribution-policies list
candidates.claim: Curated table of AI contribution policies across about 100 projects (allow or ban, disclosure, trailer form). Shows Fedify forbidding Co-authored-by for AI, among others.
candidates.limits: Manually maintained and possibly stale.
candidates.why: Quick lookup before letting an agent open PRs to someone else's repo.

candidates.name: US Copyright Office Part 2 + Thaler v. Perlmutter
candidates.claim: Purely AI-generated material is not copyrightable, and prompts alone are not sufficient control. Human selection, arrangement and modification can be protected case by case. The D.C. Circuit (March 2025) held that the Copyright Act requires human authorship.
candidates.limits: US only. Fully autonomous agent output falls on the unprotected side, but no court has applied this to code yet.
candidates.why: The legal basis for why fully autonomous agent code may be unprotectable, and why human review matters for ownership.

candidates.name: Doe v. GitHub (9th Cir. 2026)
candidates.claim: Affirmed dismissal of the DMCA 1202(b) claims. Copilot and Codex create new works rather than removing CMI from copies. The 'identicality' requirement was rejected as atextual. The input or training theory was forfeited, and the contract claims remain pending in district court.
candidates.limits: Turns on the generation-versus-retrieval architecture, so RAG or retrieval tools may be treated differently. Says nothing on ordinary infringement.
candidates.why: Reduces one statutory-damages risk for using agent-written code, while leaving license and infringement exposure open.

candidates.name: Vendor IP indemnity comparison (Microsoft CCC, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google)
candidates.claim: Microsoft's commitment requires the protected-material code filter to be on, and in annotate mode the cited license must be complied with. Third-party comparisons (beri.net, aiinsurancetracker, both November 2026) find most indemnities exclude modified or combined output and free or consumer tiers. Anthropic's commercial terms are uncapped and name training data.
candidates.limits: Comparisons are secondary readings of terms. Negotiated contracts override them. Agentic workflows almost always modify and combine output.
candidates.why: Consumer-plan coding agents carry no indemnity, which matters for employer repos.

candidates.name: LiCoEval
candidates.claim: Benchmark of 14 LLMs. 0.88-2.01% of outputs are 'strikingly similar' to existing open-source code (over 10 lines, complexity above 3, similarity above 0.6). Most models give no or wrong license info for copyleft code.
candidates.limits: Older models. The striking-similarity threshold is the authors' own.
candidates.why: About 1-2% regurgitation is the best available estimate for license contamination risk.

candidates.name: Breaking Copyleft with ChatGPT (2502.05023)
candidates.claim: Over 70k GPT-4 Java method generations. Copyleft reproduction is rare per request, but a larger matching context (copyleft code already in the class) raises it, and higher temperature lowers it. The model shows no awareness of the problem.
candidates.limits: Single model and single language.
candidates.why: Implies contamination compounds in agent loops that read already-contaminated files.

candidates.name: FOSSA Snippet Scanning
candidates.claim: Fingerprints first-party files, matches them against an open-source index, and surfaces matched package and license in an inventory and in SBOM or attribution reports. Positioned against risk from AI coding tools.
candidates.limits: Enterprise-only. Only matches known open-source code, and false positives need human rejection.
candidates.why: Enterprise cost. Relevant only if an employer mandates it.

candidates.name: Black Duck Snippet API
candidates.claim: Per-block snippet matching (about 2 seconds for 20-50 lines) in PRs via GitHub Actions, returning the matching component and license as SARIF.
candidates.limits: Commercial, with unpublished accuracy.
candidates.why: Enterprise tool.

candidates.name: cdxgen aibom / CycloneDX ML-BOM
candidates.claim: cdxgen's aibom command catalogs prompt files, AI services, MCP configs and model metadata into a CycloneDX AI-BOM, with governance audits for agent and MCP findings. It also exports SPDX 3.0.1.
candidates.limits: Inventories AI components in a repo, not provenance of which code an agent wrote.
candidates.why: An inexpensive way to inventory agent configs and MCP servers as supply-chain components.

candidates.name: coding.sh attribution
candidates.claim: Matches lines added by commits to lines added by captured agent sessions. Uses patch-id, same-file and moved-line matching with confidence levels and a 21-day window, survives rebases, and exports Agent Trace JSONL per commit.
candidates.limits: Heuristic matching after the fact. A small product with no published accuracy.
candidates.why: An alternative to hook-based recording that also emits the Agent Trace format.

candidates.name: repowise: AI code provenance overview
candidates.claim: Three-way taxonomy: trailers, session recorders (Git AI, agentdiff with ed25519-signed records, Mesa's Agent Blame in git notes, Semantica) and inference from history.

gaps: No measured accuracy for session recorders (Git AI, Agent Trace emitters). How often attribution is lost or wrong after real rebase, squash and format workflows is self-reported only.
No standard SLSA buildType or in-toto predicate for 'agent run produced this diff'. Every vendor invents its own fields, and nobody has published a verifier that blocks merge on it.
No data on whether disclosure trailers help reviewers or lower defect rates. The kernel shows low compliance, but nobody measured downstream value.

The bypass rate of install-time firewalls for freshly registered slopsquats (minutes old, before feed flagging) is unmeasured. The trade-off between minimum-age cooldowns and agent productivity is also unmeasured.
License contamination rates for 2026 frontier agent loops (multi-file, repo-context-heavy) are unknown. LiCoEval and the copyleft studies cover older single-shot models.
Whether a solo developer owns copyright in largely autonomous agent output, and how employer IP assignment interacts with it, has no case law for code.
How to reconcile attribution with privacy: session URLs and prompts in commits leak to employer or public repos, and nobody proposes redaction standards beyond Git AI's prompt store.
